verses.text: After David had finished talking with Saul, Jonathan became one in spirit with David, and he loved him as he loved himself.
From that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him go back home to his father's house.
And Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his other clothes, and even his sword, his bow and his belt.
Whatever mission Saul sent him on, David was so successful that Saul put him in charge of the soldiers. This pleased all the people, and Saul's officers as well.

When the men were coming home after David had killed the Philistine, the women came out from all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul. They sang and danced with joy, playing tambourines and other instruments.
As they danced, they sang: "Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands."
Saul was very angry. This song upset him. "They have given David tens of thousands," he thought, "but me only thousands. What more can he get but the kingdom?"
From that time on, Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day an evil spirit from God came powerfully on Saul. He was raving like a madman in his house while David was playing the harp, as he usually did. Saul had a spear in his hand,
and he threw it, saying to himself, "I will pin David to the wall." But David escaped from him twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had left Saul.
So Saul sent David away from him and made him commander over a thousand men. David led the troops in their battles.
In everything he did he had great success, because the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw how successful he was, he was even more afraid of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he led them in their battles.

Saul said to David, "Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only serve me bravely and fight the LORD's battles." Saul thought, "I will not raise a hand against him. Let the Philistines do that!"
But David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family or my father's clan in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
But when the time came for Merab, Saul's daughter, to be given to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah.
Now Saul's daughter Michal was in love with David. When Saul was told about it, he was pleased.
"I will give her to him," he thought, "so that she may be a trap for him and the Philistines may kill him." So Saul said to David, "Now you have a second chance to become my son-in-law."
Then Saul ordered his servants: "Speak to David privately and say, 'Look, the king likes you, and all his servants love you. Now become his son-in-law.'"
They repeated these words to David. But David said, "Do you think it is a small thing to become the king's son-in-law? I am only a poor man and not well known."
When Saul's servants told him what David had said,
Saul replied, "Say to David, 'The king wants no other bride price than a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on his enemies.'" Saul's plan was to have David killed by the Philistines.
When the servants told David this, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. So before the time was up,

David took his men with him and went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought back their foreskins and counted them all out to the king so that he could become the king's son-in-law. Then Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage.
When Saul realised that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved him,
he became even more afraid of David, and he remained David's enemy for the rest of his life.
The Philistine commanders kept going out to battle, and every time they did, David had more success than the rest of Saul's officers, and his name became very famous.
